kvarc-chy-granit-stilnytsia.title: Quartz or granite for a countertop: which is better in 2026
kvarc-chy-granit-stilnytsia.h1: Quartz or granite for a kitchen countertop — which to choose?
kvarc-chy-granit-stilnytsia.description: Quartz or granite for a countertop? We compare strength, care, heat, pattern and price to help you choose the material for your kitchen.
kvarc-chy-granit-stilnytsia.dek: The two most popular kitchen materials: where each wins and where it loses.
kvarc-chy-granit-stilnytsia.intro: Quartz and granite cover most requests for a kitchen countertop, but they do it differently. Granite is a natural rock with a unique pattern that calmly takes hot pans and keeps its polish for years. Quartz is an engineered material of quartz sand and resin: non-porous, consistent in colour and simpler in daily care. Below we break down the difference with examples from our workshop in Kostopil.

sections.heading: What to choose — quartz or granite?
sections.body:
The short answer: if you cook a lot, put hot pans straight on the counter and want the kitchen to have a natural character, choose granite. If an even colour, a total absence of pores and minimal care matter more, and you are used to putting hot things on a trivet, choose quartz.

This is not a question of “better or worse” but of scenario. Both materials last for decades, both are cut, polished and installed with the same technology. The difference is in how they behave in use, and that is exactly what to weigh before ordering.

sections.heading: How does engineered quartz differ from granite?
sections.body:
Granite is quarried in blocks, sawn into slabs and polished. Everything you see on the surface was made by nature: crystals of feldspar, quartz and mica, veins, inclusions. Two slabs from one block are similar but not identical.

Engineered quartz is made in a factory: roughly 90–93 % ground quartz is pressed with resin and pigments under vacuum. Hence its main properties: a surface without pores, a stable colour within a batch, “marble-look” or “concrete-look” decors. The resin also sets the limits: the material dislikes temperatures above about 150 °C and is not meant for outdoors, because ultraviolet changes the shade over time.

sections.heading: Which is stronger and more practical day to day?
sections.body:
In hardness the two materials are close: 6–7 on the Mohs scale, meaning a knife will not scratch them. The difference lies elsewhere. On granite you can forget a hot frying pan and nothing will happen. On quartz a hot base leaves a matte mark that cannot be polished out at home, so a trivet is mandatory.

Quartz has the advantage near the sink and in the cooking zone: it does not absorb water, oil, wine or beetroot juice. Granite with a good sealant behaves almost the same, but the sealant needs periodic renewal. Chips on corners are possible in both cases, and in both cases they are repaired on site.

sections.heading: Which needs less care?
sections.body:
Quartz: a soft cloth, warm water, a neutral cleaner if needed. No sealing or waxing. The only rule is no abrasives and no aggressive chemicals such as oven cleaners.

Granite: the same daily routine plus a sealant check every few months. The test is simple: a drop of water on the surface; if a dark spot appears under it after 10–15 minutes, it is time to renew the protection. We show how to do it when handing over the piece.

sections.heading: Who is granite for, and who is quartz for?
sections.body:
Granite is for those who value a natural pattern and do not want to think about heat. It belongs in homes with a large kitchen where the counter works as a worktable, and in interiors where the texture of stone matters.

Quartz is for light minimalist kitchens, for long counters without visible joints between identical slabs, for families who want the simplest possible use. It is also convenient when the colour must match the cabinet fronts exactly: the catalogue has dozens of repeatable decors from Caesarstone, Vicostone and Silestone.

rows: Granite is unique, approve the slab

faq.question: Does granite need sealing?
faq.answer: Yes, polished granite is treated with a protective sealant after installation and the procedure is repeated based on the water test, usually every one to three years. It takes half an hour and needs no professional.

faq.question: Is quartz afraid of hot pans?
faq.answer: Brief contact with a warm pot is safe, but a frying pan from the hob or a tray from the oven can leave a matte mark because of the resin. Use a trivet.

faq.question: Which is more expensive?
faq.answer: It depends on the specific stone. Ukrainian granites are usually more affordable than branded quartz, while an imported granite in a rare colour can cost more. Compare your size in the calculator.

faq.question: Which is better for a family with children?
faq.answer: Both options are safe and hygienic. Quartz is simpler because it has no pores; granite forgives heat and accidental knocks. For a light kitchen with active cooking people more often choose quartz, for a dark or natural kitchen — granite.

stilnytsia-z-kvarcytu-taj-mahal.title: Taj Mahal quartzite countertop: properties and care
stilnytsia-z-kvarcytu-taj-mahal.h1: Taj Mahal quartzite for a countertop — what to know
stilnytsia-z-kvarcytu-taj-mahal.description: Taj Mahal quartzite: natural pattern, hardness, resistance to heat and stains, care. How to approve a slab and price a countertop.
stilnytsia-z-kvarcytu-taj-mahal.dek: A light natural quartzite that looks like marble and works like granite.
stilnytsia-z-kvarcytu-taj-mahal.intro: Taj Mahal is a Brazilian quartzite of a cream-beige tone with soft golden veins. It is chosen instead of marble when you want a light natural surface without fear of lemon and wine. It is one of the hardest natural materials in our catalogue, but with a few nuances worth knowing before cutting.

sections.heading: What is quartzite and how does it differ from marble?
sections.body:
Quartzite is a metamorphic rock formed from sandstone under pressure and heat. The quartz grains have fused into a dense mass, so the material is hard, scratch-resistant and hardly reacts to acids. Outwardly it often resembles marble thanks to its wavy veins, which is exactly why the two are confused.

Marble consists of calcite. Calcite is soft and dissolves in acids: a drop of lemon juice leaves a matte spot on polished marble within minutes. Quartzite in the same situation does not change. Both stones feel cold to the touch, but quartzite is harder to scratch even with a knife.

sections.heading: Why choose Taj Mahal instead of marble?
sections.body:
The main reason is practicality without losing the look. The light warm tone and calm pattern make a kitchen or island resemble a marble interior, but the surface withstands daily cooking. The material pairs well with wood, brass and warm cabinet fronts.

The second reason is stability. Taj Mahal is quarried in large blocks, so slabs measure about 3 × 1.8 m. For long counters and islands this means fewer joints, and the veins can be continued from the top onto the edge with a 40 mm laminated edge.

sections.heading: How strong and stain-resistant is it?
sections.body:
Taj Mahal's hardness is around 7 on the Mohs scale, the level of granite and above. Hot pans do not harm it, and chips on corners are rare given a correct edge profile.

As for stains: quartzite has micropores, so after installation we always seal the surface. Without sealing, oil or wine can leave a shadow; with sealing the surface behaves like quartz. Important: not all stones called “quartzite” are the same. Some soft varieties contain calcite and behave like marble, so we check every slab with an acid test on the edge before cutting.

sections.heading: How do you care for quartzite?
sections.body:
Daily: warm water, a soft cloth, a neutral stone cleaner. Wipe up spills right away, especially coloured liquids on a light surface. Abrasive powders and metal scourers are unnecessary and harmful to the polish.

Every six months do a water test. If a drop soaks in within 10–15 minutes, renew the sealant: apply it with a sponge, let it work and wipe dry. A honed finish is sealed more often than a polished one, because its surface is more open.

rows: Fewer joints on a long counter

faq.question: Is quartzite natural or artificial?
faq.answer: Natural. It is often confused with engineered quartz, but quartzite is quarried in blocks, not made in a factory.

faq.question: Can I put hot things on it?
faq.answer: Yes. Quartzite takes hot pans without consequences. The only caution concerns sudden local heating at a glued joint, which is why we do not place joints next to the hob.

faq.question: Does it darken from water?
faq.answer: Unsealed quartzite can temporarily darken from water, like granite, and dry without a trace. After sealing, water stays as a drop on the surface. That is the test for whether the protection needs renewing.

faq.question: Is it suitable for an island?
faq.answer: It is one of the best options for an island: the large slab format allows a 2.5–3 m counter without joints, and a 40–60 mm laminated edge gives a massive look without extra weight.

tovshchyna-stilnytsi-20-30-mm.title: Stone countertop thickness: 20 or 30 mm?
tovshchyna-stilnytsi-20-30-mm.h1: Which countertop thickness to choose — 20 or 30 mm?
tovshchyna-stilnytsi-20-30-mm.description: 20 or 30 mm for a stone countertop: rigidity, weight, overhangs, edge look and cost. When 20 mm is enough and how to make a thick edge.
tovshchyna-stilnytsi-20-30-mm.dek: Thickness as a structural and visual decision for a countertop.
tovshchyna-stilnytsi-20-30-mm.intro: Most natural stone in Ukraine is sold in 20 and 30 mm slabs, quartz in 20 and 30 mm, porcelain in 6, 12 and 20 mm. Thickness determines not only the look of the edge but also weight, permissible overhangs, requirements for the kitchen carcass and price. We explain how we choose thickness in the workshop and when a “thin” countertop is actually better.

sections.heading: Which thickness is optimal?
sections.body:
For a kitchen countertop on standard 600 mm deep units, 20 mm is optimal. That thickness is enough for strength, cut-outs for the sink and hob, and the weight stays moderate: about 55 kg per linear metre for granite.

30 mm is chosen for two reasons: structural (long overhangs, stairs, exterior details, heavy sinks on wide spans) or visual (a massive edge without lamination). If only the look is needed, it is cheaper and lighter to make 20 mm with a laminated edge of up to 40–60 mm.

sections.heading: What does countertop thickness depend on?
sections.body:
On the material, the spans between supports and what will stand on the counter. Granite and quartzite are rigid, quartz is more flexible and works well at 20 mm even with long overhangs. Marble is softer, so on wide spans we prefer 30 mm or reinforce 20 mm with an aluminium profile underneath.

The supports matter too: a solid top on the units or just a frame, whether there is a bar console without legs, whether built-in appliances with a cut-out right at the edge are planned. Every cut-out weakens the slab, and the bridge next to it must be no narrower than 50–70 mm.

sections.heading: How does 20 mm differ from 30 mm?
sections.body:
Weight: 30 mm is one and a half times heavier. For a long island that is a difference of several tens of kilograms that the carcass must bear and that must be carried upstairs without a lift.

Overhangs: without reinforcement 20 mm safely gives a cantilever of about 250–300 mm, 30 mm — up to 350–400 mm. Bar overhangs beyond that need steel plates in grooves or brackets.

Look: a 30 mm edge reads as massive, 20 mm as light and modern. The edge profile on 30 mm has more options: half bullnose, ogee, full bullnose.

sections.heading: How does thickness affect the look and cost?
sections.body:
A 30 mm slab costs more than 20 mm, and edge work on a thick slab takes longer. For most kitchens the difference in the final estimate is 20 to 40 %, so we offer 30 mm only where the structure justifies it.

A 40 mm laminated edge from 20 mm material gives the look of a thick slab for less money and weight. With correct cutting the joint is almost invisible, especially on uniform materials and quartz. On stones with pronounced veins we select a strip from the same zone of the slab so the pattern continues.

sections.heading: What to consider for the hob and sink?
sections.body:
We hang an undermount sink from the slab on brackets, so around the cut-out we leave at least 60 mm of stone to the edge and round the corners with a 10–15 mm radius to relieve stress. This rule is the same for 20 and 30 mm.

Hob: the cut-out must be set back 50–70 mm from the rear edge, and between the hob and the sink a solid section of at least 300 mm is needed, otherwise the slab has to be split. For induction we additionally check the depth of the unit under it so the body does not press against the frame.

rows: 20 mm for kitchens, 30 mm for stairs
About 55 and 80 kg per lin. m of granite
Check the carcass and the carry-in
20 mm up to 300 mm, 30 mm up to 400 mm

faq.question: Is 20 mm enough for a kitchen?
faq.answer: Yes, in the vast majority of kitchens 20 mm is the standard: it takes the sink, the hob and daily load. 30 mm is needed for long consoles or a massive style.

faq.question: How is a thick edge made?
faq.answer: A strip of the same stone is glued to the underside of the 20 mm slab, the edge is polished and you get a 40 mm edge. The joint runs along the bottom edge and is not visible at eye level.

faq.question: What is better for minimalism?
faq.answer: For a thin modern look choose 20 mm or 12 mm porcelain with a straight edge. For a “heavy” Scandinavian or loft style — 30 mm or laminated 60 mm.

faq.question: Is a non-standard thickness possible?
faq.answer: Yes: by laminating two or three layers you get an edge of 60, 80 or even 100 mm. The slab itself stays 20 mm, so the weight does not grow proportionally.

ukrainski-granity-porivnyannya.title: Ukrainian granites: comparing types and colours
ukrainski-granity-porivnyannya.h1: Ukrainian granites — which to choose for your project
ukrainski-granity-porivnyannya.description: An overview of Ukrainian granites: Pokostivka, gabbro, labradorite, Maple Red, Rosso Santiago and others. Colours, properties, radiation class, applications.
ukrainski-granity-porivnyannya.dek: Ten Ukrainian stones for interiors, facades and landscaping.
ukrainski-granity-porivnyannya.intro: Ukraine has some of the largest granite reserves in Europe, and most quarries are in the Zhytomyr region, a few hours from our workshop. Local stone is cheaper than imports, no worse in quality and has a documented radiation class. We explain how the ten stones in our catalogue differ and where each is best used.

sections.heading: Which Ukrainian granite to choose?
sections.body:
For countertops, stairs and any detail touched daily, the most common choice is Pokostivka granite Grey Ukraine: a calm light grey tone, fine grain, stable quality. For contrasting black surfaces — Kometa Black gabbro. For an accent with crystalline sparkle — Volga Blue labradorite.

Red and pink stones (Maple Red, Rosso Santiago, Star of Ukraine, Flower of Ukraine, Leopard) work on facades, plinths, stairs and paving, where a warm colour and high wear resistance are needed.

sections.heading: How do Pokostivka, gabbro and labradorite differ?
sections.body:
Pokostivka granite is a classic granite rock: quartz, feldspar and mica, a light grey fine-grained body. It polishes well, tolerates flaming, and suits both exterior and interior. The most versatile stone in the catalogue.

Gabbro (Kometa Black) is a dark igneous rock with fine grain. The polished surface is almost black with thin grey inclusions. Flamed gabbro becomes dark grey and matte and works excellently on entrance steps.

Labradorite (Volga Blue, Irina Blue) is a rock with large crystals that flash blue or green at an angle. It is a decorative stone for countertops, bar tops and fireplace cladding. In hardness it is no less than granite, but because of the large crystals it needs a careful edge profile.

sections.heading: Which colours are available?
sections.body:
Grey: Grey Ukraine (Pokostivka). Black: Kometa Black (gabbro). Black-blue: Volga Blue, Irina Blue. Reds: Maple Red (Leznyky), Rosso Santiago (Kapustyne), Carpazi (Tokivske). Pinks and brown-pinks: Star of Ukraine (Didkovychi), Flower of Ukraine (Mezhyrich), Leopard (Kornyn).

The shade within one quarry varies from batch to batch, so at the workshop we show photos and video of the very slab that will go into your piece, and large facade batches are selected from one block.

sections.heading: What about the radiation class and where can it be used?
sections.body:
Every natural stone contains traces of natural radionuclides. Under the DSTU standards building materials are divided into classes: class I (up to 370 Bq/kg) is allowed for any use, including housing; class II (up to 740 Bq/kg) — only for road and industrial construction and exterior work.

Most granites in our catalogue are class I, confirmed by a certificate for the batch. Tokivske granite Carpazi belongs to class II, so we sell it exclusively for outdoors: paving, plinths, retaining walls. The certificate for the specific batch is provided with the invoice.

sections.heading: Which granite for interiors and which for exteriors?
sections.body:
Interior: Grey Ukraine, Kometa Black, Volga Blue, Irina Blue, Maple Red, Rosso Santiago, Star of Ukraine — polished or honed finish, countertops, window sills, stairs, fireplace surrounds.

Exterior: all of the above plus Flower of Ukraine, Leopard and Carpazi. For outdoors choose a flamed or bush-hammered finish: it is not slippery in rain and frost, and the colour becomes calmer, one or two tones lighter than polished.

rows: Maple Red / Rosso Santiago / Star of Ukraine

faq.question: Which granite is the hardest?
faq.answer: Gabbro and labradorite are slightly denser than classic granites, but in practice the difference is not noticeable: all stones in the catalogue have a hardness of 6–7 on Mohs and a compressive strength above 180 MPa.

faq.question: Which colour is the most popular?
faq.answer: For countertops and stairs in private homes — grey Grey Ukraine, for accents — black Kometa Black. Red stones more often go to facades and paving.

faq.question: Is granite safe in the home?
faq.answer: Yes, if it is radiation class I stone with a certificate for the batch. We do not use class II materials in interiors and provide a document with every delivery.

faq.question: Which granite for a facade?
faq.answer: Any from the catalogue, provided it has a flamed or bush-hammered finish and mechanical fixing. Most often Grey Ukraine is chosen for its calm colour and Maple Red for contrasting plinths.

keramogranit-laminam-neolith-stilnytsia.title: Laminam/Neolith porcelain countertop: pros and cons
keramogranit-laminam-neolith-stilnytsia.h1: Porcelain for a countertop — when it is the best choice
keramogranit-laminam-neolith-stilnytsia.description: Laminam, Neolith, Dekton porcelain for a countertop: heat resistance, thinness, UV stability, chipping risk and installation requirements.
keramogranit-laminam-neolith-stilnytsia.dek: Large-format thin slabs in countertops and facades.
keramogranit-laminam-neolith-stilnytsia.intro: Large-format porcelain came to kitchens from facades: a 1600 × 3200 mm slab 6–12 mm thick weighs half as much as stone and fears nothing that happens in a kitchen. At the same time it is the most demanding material in our catalogue to install. We break down when it is justified and when quartz or granite is the better choice.

sections.heading: Who is porcelain for?
sections.body:
For those who need a surface you can put hot things on, cut on without a board and not think about stains. Porcelain is sintered at over 1200 °C, so it has no resins or pores: neither a frying pan, nor wine, nor ultraviolet affects it.

It also suits long countertops with a minimum of joints, thin “floating” shelves and facades where weight matters. A 12 mm slab in a kitchen looks light and modern, and the decors mimic marble, concrete or metal.

sections.heading: What are the advantages of large-format slabs?
sections.body:
The 3200 × 1600 mm format covers an L-shaped kitchen countertop with one joint. A thin 12 mm or 20 mm edge gives a graphic look, and a 45° mitred laminated edge hides the white body of the slab.

Weight: a 12 mm slab weighs about 30 kg per m² versus 55–60 kg for granite. This eases installation on old furniture, on walls and in flats without a lift. The decor is stable within a batch, so the kitchen can be extended a year later with the same collection.

sections.heading: What are the drawbacks and what to watch for?
sections.body:
Brittle edges. Porcelain withstands impact on the face but chips from a blow to the edge, especially on a straight edge. So we recommend a bevel or rounding and do not make sharp external corners.

Substrate requirements. A 6 mm slab needs continuous support over the whole area; 12 mm takes the frame of the units, but pads are still needed near cut-outs. Cut-outs for the sink and hob are cut only on a water-cooled machine; nothing can be trimmed on site.

Repair. A chip on porcelain repairs worse than on stone: a polymer insert is noticeable on uniform decors. So care in use matters more than with granite.

sections.heading: How are Laminam and Neolith better than ordinary tiles?
sections.body:
Ordinary floor porcelain is a 600 × 600 mm tile 8–10 mm thick, designed to be laid on adhesive. Large-format Laminam, Neolith and Dekton slabs are made on different equipment: they have flat geometry along the whole length, through-body colour in some collections and certification for food contact.

Dekton is technically not porcelain but an ultra-compact surface of sintered minerals, yet in properties and installation it behaves the same. All three brands give a material warranty on condition of installation by a certified fabricator, which our workshop is.

rows: Thin slabs need a continuous substrate
Chipping risk on a sharp edge

faq.question: Can I put hot things on it?
faq.answer: Yes, without limits: the material contains no resins and does not change at the temperatures a home kitchen produces.

faq.question: Does it scratch?
faq.answer: The surface is harder than a knife blade and does not scratch. The exception is matte and textured decors, on which metal cookware can leave grey marks that wash off.

faq.question: What thickness?
faq.answer: For countertops we take 12 mm with a laminated edge or 20 mm solid. 6 mm we use for wall cladding, furniture fronts and splashbacks.

faq.question: Is it suitable for facades and outdoors?
faq.answer: Yes, it is one of the best materials for ventilated facades and outdoor kitchens: it does not fade, does not absorb water and withstands frost.

marmur-u-vanniy-kimnati.title: Marble in the bathroom: pros and cons
marmur-u-vanniy-kimnati.h1: Marble in the bathroom — is it worth it and how to choose
marmur-u-vanniy-kimnati.description: Marble in the bathroom: advantages, risks, care and which varieties to choose. Bianco Carrara, Crema Marfil or Nero Marquina — which is better for a wet zone.
marmur-u-vanniy-kimnati.dek: How to design a wet zone with natural marble.
marmur-u-vanniy-kimnati.intro: The bathroom is the best place for marble in the home. There are no hot pans or knives here, but there is water, soft light and a desire for calm, which this stone was made for. Problems with marble in the bathroom arise not from the material but from the wrong detailing, acidic cosmetics and cleaners for sanitary ware. We explain how to avoid them.

sections.heading: Is marble suitable for a bathroom?
sections.body:
Yes, on three conditions. First: the surface is treated with a protective sealant and it is renewed once a year. Second: all joints on the countertop and at the walls are sealed, and the floor slopes to the drain. Third: no acid-based products are used in the home to remove limescale from the stone.

Under these conditions a marble vanity top, window sill or wall cladding lasts for decades. Italian and Spanish bathrooms with century-old marble are the proof.

sections.heading: What are the advantages of marble in a bathroom?
sections.body:
Pattern. No engineered material repeats the depth of Carrara veins or the warmth of Crema Marfil. Marble gives a spa feeling even in a small room.

Coolness and hygiene. Polished marble wipes easily, does not collect dust, and a top for a countertop basin is made without joints on the visible plane.

Compatibility. Marble pairs with brass, chrome, wood and microcement. One stone can run across the vanity top, window sill and shower shelf, and the room becomes whole.

sections.heading: What are the risks and how to avoid them?
sections.body:
Acid etching. Lemon, vinegar, limescale removers and some cosmetics leave matte spots on polished marble. Solution: neutral stone chemistry and a honed finish, on which marks are almost invisible.

Stains from oils and dyes. Body oils, hair dye, cream can penetrate the pores. Solution: sealing after installation and quick wiping.

Water in the joints. This is a problem of joints, not marble. Solution: an epoxy or silicone joint, waterproofing of the substrate under tiles, a slope on the floor. We make vanity tops with or without an upstand, depending on the detail.

sections.heading: Which varieties to choose — Bianco Carrara, Crema Marfil or Nero Marquina?
sections.body:
Bianco Carrara: a light grey background with soft grey veins. The most versatile, hides water and marks, looks good honed. Suitable for tops and walls.

Crema Marfil: cream-beige, warm, almost without contrast. Makes the room look bigger, hides limescale. One of the most practical marbles for wet zones.

Nero Marquina: black with white veins. Very striking, but every drop shows on it after drying, as do acid marks. We recommend it for walls, shelves and accents, and for a vanity top only if you are ready to wipe it dry.

rows: The most practical for a wet zone

faq.question: Is marble afraid of water?
faq.answer: No. Water does not destroy marble; acids and dirt entering the pores do. Sealed stone in a bathroom behaves like any other surface.

faq.question: How often to seal?
faq.answer: Once a year for the top and floor, once every two years for walls. The guide is the water test: if a drop soaks in within a few minutes, it is time to renew the protection.

faq.question: What to do with an acid mark?
faq.answer: A matte acid mark is not dirt but an etched surface. Small marks on honed marble are barely visible; on polished marble a craftsman removes them by grinding and polishing on site.

faq.question: What can replace marble?
faq.answer: Taj Mahal quartzite, if you need a light natural stone without acid sensitivity, or quartz or porcelain with a marble decor, if a total absence of pores matters.
